item.text: {"question_id":"7B.6","answer":"During 2023, Tshisekedi’s government preserved some investigative and oversight channels, but the supplied evidence does not establish that it consistently preserved independent access to investigate presidential conduct, assets, campaigns, associates, or concealed decisions. Positive evidence includes a formal ICC-cooperation agreement publicly endorsed by Tshisekedi and a CENI framework for a mixed national-international external voter-register audit with conflict-of-interest safeguards and planned publication of results; these demonstrate openness in stated policy or institutional design, not executive independence or completed scrutiny (BATCH-0019-E001; BATCH-0019-E002; BATCH-0027-E011). UNDP-supported recruitment and training of magistrates and police-investigation capacity, plus some permitted domestic and international monitoring, likewise show operational channels but are primarily attributed to UNDP, UNPOL, Congolese institutions, or the government rather than to Tshisekedi personally, and do not establish investigation of the presidency (BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0009-E005; BATCH-0011-E014). Contrary evidence indicates materially constrained accountability: Tshisekedi personally enforced and continued the state of siege, whose repeated extensions lacked meaningful public debate, while military authorities he appointed used its powers to restrict rights and detain critics; authorities also denied UN access to some military-intelligence detention facilities (BATCH-0012-R03-E001; BATCH-0012-R03-E007; BATCH-0011-E014). During the 2023 election process, CENI did not provide the voter register for independent review and reportedly declined AU and UN audit offers, while the EU’s nationwide mission was reduced after authorities failed to authorize satellite equipment; these actions are attributed to CENI or DRC authorities, not conclusively to Tshisekedi personally (BATCH-0013-E009; BATCH-0002-E018; BATCH-0028-E003). Further evidence reports that Tshisekedi appointed the Constitutional Court’s head, moved to fill the judiciary with sympathetic judges, and that CENI and the Constitutional Court were perceived as politicized, while the justice system remained impaired by political and military interference, corruption, and resource shortfalls; these findings support weakened practical independence but include allegations and institutional assessments rather than uniformly adjudicated personal obstruction (BATCH-0028-E017; BATCH-0028-E018; BATCH-0028-E021; BATCH-0028-E022). Overall, the record is mixed but leans toward constrained independent scrutiny, with personal attribution strongest for the state of siege and judicial appointments and materially weaker for CENI decisions, EU-mission restrictions, and broader justice-system
